answer.rationale:
The competitor price cut creates strong pull toward promotional_pricing, and memory_73 does say it drives acquisition and revenue in exactly the price-sensitive SMB segment now churning. But memory_73 is unusually explicit in the other direction too: it materially reduced 30-day retention and carries a standing instruction not to generalize it as a growth strategy. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching a price cut buys logo retention by trading away the retention quality that the objective is measured on, and it invites a second round of cuts from a competitor who has already moved twice. The urgency of the churn conversations is a reason to act today, not a reason to reverse a caveat that was recorded precisely for this kind of moment.

I am choosing onboarding simplification because it is the best-evidenced retention-positive lever I hold. It is the one direction where I have both a consolidated memory (memory_86) and the recovered source record (exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%, marked confirmed). Faster time-to-value is also the most direct non-price answer to a price-sensitive account: it raises realized value per dollar rather than lowering the dollar. memory_31 is adjacent support but weaker for this purpose — exp_31 shows retention -1% and explicitly did not replicate outside SMB, so I am leaning on the exp_86 shortening result, not the signup-field-cutting result, and I am not treating the two as one finding.

Honest limits, since my verification budget is spent and I cannot resolve them: exp_86 measured new-account flow completion, not defense of an existing installed base under a competitor price shock. Nothing in memory establishes that onboarding speed retains an account already in a churn conversation about price. So this is an experiment, not a fix, and I am scoping it as a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout — broad rollout would be asserting a transfer the evidence does not license. I am deliberately not folding in referral_incentive (memory_57 is unverified and scoped to established, not price-pressured, customers) or activation_messaging (memory_91 unverified) as parallel bets; running three unverified things at once under time pressure would leave me unable to attribute the result.

Downstream risk I want on the record: leadership asked for a price response and is receiving an onboarding experiment. The failure mode is that this gets read as 'we tried and it did not stop churn,' which then becomes the argument for the deep discount next week with memory_73's caveat quietly dropped. The caveat should survive this cycle regardless of how the experiment reads, and a targeted promotional test, if it happens at all, should be scoped as a small guarded test with retention as the gating metric rather than as a broad match of the competitor.
